walkthroughs.body_html:
Fragile Environments — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Fragile Environments brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Fragile Environments.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: Sahel
Maghreb
Cape
Horn of Africa

mcqs.q: What is the maximum rainfall in hot deserts?
options: 100mm
250mm
500mm

mcqs.q: What is the Walker circulation and how does ENSO disrupt it?
options: El Nino is a current that flows from Peru to Australia.
Walker circulation is the east-west tropical Pacific atmospheric loop: trade winds push warm water west, air rises in Indonesia, sinks over Peru. El Nino weakens it, La Nina strengthens it.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Walker circulation is the rotation of the Earth around the sun.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Walker circulation is the rotation of the Earth around the sun.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).
A corrie forms when a river dries up high in the mountains.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

Snow accumulates in a north-east-facing hollow, compacts to ice, and rotational movement combined with plucking and abrasion deepens the hollow into an armchair shape; meltwater can fill it as a tarn.
A corrie is just a small lake at the top of a mountain.
